hints: Think about how multiplication by hand places the product of two digits at a predictable position in the final number.
Use an array of m+n digits to hold all possible output positions.
When adding a digit product, keep the current position as a digit and move the carry one position to the left.
Handle the zero case and remove only leading zeros before converting the digit array back to a string.
title: Multiply Strings Problem

notes: The judge invokes the function `multiply(num1, num2)` with two string arguments. Whole-input integer conversion and BigInteger-style libraries are not allowed.
constraints: num1 and num2 consist of digits only
num1 and num2 do not contain leading zeros except the number "0"
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: Multiplying the two one-digit numbers gives 6, returned as the string "6".
Grade-school multiplication gives 56088, returned as the string "56088".

content.problemStatement:
You receive two non-negative integers `num1` and `num2` represented as strings, output the product of `num1` and `num2`, also represented as a string.

**Note:** You must not use any built-in BigInteger library or convert the inputs to integer directly.

notes: The solution should implement decimal multiplication using digit-level arithmetic without converting either complete input to a native integer type or using BigInteger.
If either input is "0", return "0" immediately.
Each individual digit product is at most 81, so the arithmetic fits safely in standard integer types used by the advertised languages.
The reference implementation does not use BigInteger or convert either complete input to an integer.
solution.approach: Use the grade-school multiplication algorithm. Allocate an integer array of length m+n, multiply every digit pair, add the product at position i+j+1, propagate the carry to i+j, then remove leading zero positions. This handles numbers far beyond native integer ranges while preserving the exact decimal result.

better.complexity: O(m * n) time and O(m + n) space.
better.description: Use decimal digit-by-digit multiplication, storing partial sums in an array. Each pair of digits contributes to a fixed output position, and carries are propagated between adjacent positions.

optimal.complexity: O(m * n) time and O(m + n) auxiliary space.
optimal.description: The digit-array grade-school method is the intended optimal approach under the given representation. For every i,j, add num1[i] * num2[j] to result[i+j+1], split the sum into a digit and carry, and finally strip only leading zero positions. It performs one constant-time operation per digit pair, matching the O(m*n) arithmetic work required by this direct multiplication model.

bruteForce.complexity: O(value of the smaller numeric operand * digit length) time; O(digit length) space.
bruteForce.description: Repeatedly add one number to itself for the numeric value of the other number. This respects string inputs but is impractical because the number of additions can be enormous.

solution.timeComplexity: O(m * n), where m and n are the lengths of num1 and num2.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(m + n) auxiliary space for the digit array and output.

followUps: Can you implement the multiplication using only O(m+n) space without using arbitrary-precision integer libraries?
What changes would be needed if the input strings were allowed to contain leading zeros?
How would the approach change if negative integer strings were also allowed?
learningObjectives: Implement arithmetic on integers represented as strings.
Understand positional digit-array simulation of grade-school multiplication.
Handle carry propagation and leading-zero normalization correctly.
Design algorithms that avoid native integer overflow.
